claims.text: A JSON value is an object, an array, a string, a number, or one of the literals true, false and null; there is no other kind of value.
claims.source_hint: RFC 8259 §3 Values (not pinned in versions.yaml; see open_questions)

claims.text: It has no date type, so a date usually travels as a string that both sides agree to read as a date.
claims.source_hint: RFC 8259 §3; .NET docs 'DateTime and DateTimeOffset support in System.Text.Json' (dates written as ISO 8601 strings)

claims.text: JSON has no comment syntax; System.Text.Json does not allow comments in JSON by default.
claims.source_hint: RFC 8259 §2 grammar; refs/dotnet-docs .../system-text-json/invalid-json.md 'Allow comments and trailing commas'

claims.text: JSON has a single number kind: the text 3 does not mark itself as integer or decimal, and the type of the field that receives it decides how it is read.
claims.source_hint: RFC 8259 §6 Numbers (one number grammar, no integer/decimal distinction; interpretation left to implementations)

claims.text: JSON text exchanged between separate systems (RFC 8259: systems that are not part of a closed ecosystem) must be encoded using UTF-8.
claims.source_hint: RFC 8259 §8.1 Character Encoding

claims.text: There, a space or a plain English letter such as N takes one byte, while Đ takes two and ẵ takes three; so Đà Nẵng is 7 characters and 11 bytes: c4 90 c3 a0 20 4e e1 ba b5 6e 67.
claims.source_hint: outputs/stage-0/scripts/http/post-json.txt lines 11-16 (wc -m, wc -c, od); RFC 3629 §3 UTF-8 definition

claims.text: Content-Length gives the length of the body as a number of bytes (octets), not characters; the lab's 40-byte body has 40 characters because each of them takes one byte in UTF-8.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 §8.6 Content-Length; outputs/stage-0/scripts/http/post-json.txt lines 7 and 9

claims.text: The Content-Type header indicates the media type of the body, which defines its data format and how the recipient is meant to process it; application/json names JSON.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 §8.3 Content-Type; RFC 8259 §11 (application/json registration)

claims.text: 415 Unsupported Media Type means the server refuses the request because its content is in a format it does not support; the problem may come from the indicated Content-Type or from inspecting the data.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 §15.5.16 415 Unsupported Media Type

claims.text: 400 Bad Request is the general answer to a request the server perceives as a client error; a server can use it for a body labelled JSON that breaks JSON's rules.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 §15.5.1 400 Bad Request

claims.text: Decoding with an encoding that reads one byte as one character, such as ISO-8859-1, turns each letter that took several bytes into two or three wrong characters, one per byte, some invisible, while plain English letters stay the same.
